content.title: Full list of Artemis II launch windows: See backup times for liftoff
content.text: Updated March 31, 2026, 5:23 p.m. ET3, 2, 1... liftoff!That's what NASA engineers are planning to hear on Wednesday evening, April 1, when the historic Artemis II launch is set to send four astronauts from the Kennedy Space Center near Cape Canaveral, Florida, toward the moon's orbit. It's an important step in the U.S. effort to return to the lunar surface for the first time in more than half a century.The second mission under the U.S. space agency's multibillion-dollar Artemis program, Artemis II only has a few possible dates it can set off on its journey. That's due to a bit of science and technology.If the first launch opportunity gets called off, NASA has a handful of backup options. Here's a look at NASA's launch windows and how to tune in here on Earth.What are the possible launch times?NASA's first chance to send off Artemis II's crew is on Wednesday, April 1, with a two-hour launch window opening at 6:24 p.m. ET. If bad weather comes up or any other facet of the launch technology goes awry, the crew can attempt launch again during two-hour windows between April 2 and 6 and also on April 30.NASA's two-hour launch windows for Artemis II begin at the following times:April 1: 6:24 p.m. EDTApril 2: 7:22 p.m. EDTApril 3: 8:00 p.m. EDTApril 4: 8:53 p.m. EDTApril 5: 9:40 p.m. EDTApril 6: 10:36 p.m. EDTApril 30: 6:06 p.m. EDTNASA officials said at a news conference March 31 that the backup launch opportunities looked "somewhat less favorable for weather" than the initial April 1 window.Why does the launch have a limited window?Artemis II's launch is limited to specific dates and hours due to what's called an "orbital window," the time the launch can happen successfully.In all space missions, this window is subject to various constraints based on the kind of space vehicle launching and where it's determined to go, according to NASA.The window could be shortened to just a few hours, as is the case with Artemis II, because the launch needs Earth's rotational motion to launch the rocket on its path. Remember: Earth and the moon are simultaneously spinning as the launch happens, so scientists have to align their positions to send Artemis II on its correct trajectory. We wouldn't want to miss the moon!Now will be the time to put preparation for the launch window into action. The launch date got back on track last month after a simulation showed hydrogen fuel leaks within the rocket's 212-foot core stage. NASA engineers scrambled to get back on schedule, making fixes to the 322-foot rocket.Now, scientists wait for the ideal weather, technical criteria and orbital positions to all line up. If those boxes are ticked, the countdown begins.Here's how to watch the launch liveTune into all-day coverage by NASA on April 1 of Artemis II preparations leading up to the launch.Livestreams will be available throughout the day on Amazon Prime, NASA's YouTube channel and NASA+, the agency's free streaming service.Contributing: Eric Lagatta, USA TODAY
